problem.text: Credit card delinquency and default pose financial risk to lenders, and credit risk must often be assessed for customers with limited or no credit history.
Customer payment data is heavily imbalanced because most customers pay on time and only a small share default, which makes predictive modelling harder.

objectives.text: Build a contemporary credit scoring model that forecasts credit defaults for unsecured lending (credit cards) using machine learning.
Evaluate and compare popular classification models on publicly available data to find the most efficient and best-performing one for predicting default and delinquency.

methodology.text: Two datasets, customer personal details and credit history, were analysed and merged into one dataset with 17 features.
Seven categorical variables were converted to numbers with a Label Encoder.
SMOTE, an oversampling method based on K-Nearest Neighbors, was used to balance the training data.
The merged data was split 70% for training and 30% for testing.
Models were compared using accuracy score and AUC of the ROC curve, with precision, recall and F1 defined as supporting metrics in a classification report.
The number of models compared is reported inconsistently: seven in the abstract and Section 4.1, but six in the Introduction and Conclusion.

dataset.text: The application set holds customer personal details described by 18 labeled variables, including gender, income, education, family status, housing and occupation.
The credit history set has 1,048,575 rows and 3 variables (ID, monthly balance, payment status) capturing each customer's monthly dues.
The data comes from publicly available datasets, with the Kaggle datasets site cited as the source.
Table 2 coding is inconsistent: the text says a Monthly Balance of 0 means no payment delay, but Status code 0 is listed as 1-29 days past due.

algorithms.text: The models described are Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost and LGBM, though the text names only six in the Introduction.
The LGBM tuning hyperparameters discussed are max_depth, learning_rate and num_leaves.
The SVM section calls SVM a linear model yet describes a gamma hyperparameter, which applies to kernel SVMs, so the description is inconsistent.
The paper says max_depth is inversely proportional to overfitting, which contradicts its own advice to reduce max_depth when overfitting is detected.

results.text: Table 3 reports test accuracy of 0.5579 for Logistic Regression, 0.6947 for SVM, 0.7677 for KNN, 0.8145 for Decision Tree, 0.8587 for Random Forest, 0.9196 for XGBoost and 0.9553 for LGBM.
LGBM has the highest accuracy and is reported with an AUC of 0.99, with XGBoost and LGBM named as the best ROC fits.
LGBM accuracy conflicts within the paper: the Conclusion text says 95.35% while Table 3 gives 0.9552716 (95.53%).
The claim that LGBM is statistically better than other classifiers is not backed by any reported statistical test or AUC values for the other models.

limitations.text: The paper notes that AUROC does not capture performance properly on datasets with far more negative than positive examples.

The paper acknowledges that the credit dataset is not large enough for LGBM, which it says typically handles datasets above 10,000 data values, so the stated threshold conflicts with its own 1,048,575-row dataset.

future_work.text: The paper suggests the model could be further optimized by fine-tuning max_depth, learning_rate and num_leaves.

analysis.summary: The paper tries to predict credit card defaults using machine learning, handling the fact that very few customers default by creating extra synthetic examples of defaulters with SMOTE. It compares several classifiers on public customer and credit-history data and finds that LGBM scores highest, with about 95.5% accuracy in Table 3, though the Conclusion text says 95.35% and the paper is inconsistent about whether it compared six or seven models. Claims that LGBM is faster, uses less memory, is statistically better, or beats all prior work are not backed by any measurements or tests in the paper, so they should not be treated as results.
